title: Karma of the yogi — neither white nor black (4.7)
hook: most people's actions come in three colors; Patanjali says the yogi's come in none

segments.voice: Yesterday, sutras 4.2 to 4.6: kshetrika. Your line was the farmer removes the barrier. Practice doesn't push the water; it opens the channel. Did you clear one small blockage and let something flow? Day four hundred eighty-two.

Laundry day. Three piles on the bedroom floor: the whites, the darks, and the big mixed heap that's a bit of both. Everything goes somewhere. Patanjali sorts human action the same way, by color, and he names the piles. Then, in one short line of the fourth chapter, he says something that sounds strange at first: the action of a person who has gone all the way in yoga goes in no pile at all.
screen: `THREE PILES ON THE FLOOR.` → `ACTION, SORTED BY COLOR.` → `AND ONE KIND IN NO PILE.`

segments.voice: Here's the thread, sutra 4.7: karma ashukla-akrishnam yoginas, trividham itaresham. The action of the yogi is not white and not black. For everyone else, it is of three kinds. Shukla means white, or bright. Krishna here means black, or dark. The old commentary attributed to Vyasa spells out the three. Black is action that harms. Black-and-white, mixed, is ordinary action: it does good, but it leans on outward means and touches others, so it's never perfectly clean. White is action done inwardly, through discipline, study and meditation. All three leave seeds. Bright seeds and dark seeds, but seeds, and seeds sprout. That's the surprise. For Patanjali, white karma isn't the finish line. A gold chain still holds you. So what is the fourth kind, neither white nor black? The commentators describe someone whose afflictions have worn thin, who acts without craving the fruit. The act still happens. Food gets cooked, the sick get visited. But nothing new is being sown, because nobody is standing there waiting for the harvest. If that sounds familiar, it's close to what Krishna tells Arjuna in the Gita: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. Patanjali puts it in his own terms. Action without the hook of wanting leaves no seed behind. So the line isn't saying the yogi stops caring about good and harm. It says the yogi's good is done without a hand held out.
screen: `WHITE, BLACK, AND MIXED.` · `ALL THREE LEAVE SEEDS.` · `A GOLD CHAIN STILL HOLDS YOU.` · `NEITHER: ACTION WITHOUT THE HAND OUT.` · then, large: `KARMĀŚUKLĀKṚṢṆAṂ YOGINAS TRIVIDHAM ITAREṢĀM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one kind thing you did recently. Notice whether anything is attached to it: a wish to be thanked, to be seen as good, to have it count. Don't fight that wish. Just see it, the way you'd see a sticker left on a piece of fruit. Then let the act stand by itself, without the sticker. It happened. It was good. That's enough. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Ashukla-akrishna, neither white nor black. The yogi's karma, done fully and left free of its fruit, so it plants no seed.
Your line: neither. Today, do one good thing that nobody will ever know about, and don't mention it, not even to yourself at the end of the day. Day four hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often read 4.7 alongside the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on action without attachment to its fruit, and some practitioners try to do service quietly, without seeking credit.

pairs: the yogi's action, free of fruit

myth: for Patanjali, white karma is the final goal
white karma still leaves seeds. the yogi's action is neither white nor black.
sutra 4.7 says everyone else's karma is of three kinds
trividham itaresham: threefold for the others.
the yogi in 4.7 stops acting altogether

fork.setup: Patanjali sorts action by color. which kind does he give to the yogi?
fork.reveal: neither. even bright karma leaves seeds; the yogi's action, done without craving its fruit, leaves none.

original.note: Sanskrit: a (not) + shukla (white) + a (not) + krishna (black). neither white nor black.

trapdoor: what you thought: yoga is about piling up good karma.
what it means: good and bad karma both leave seeds; the yogi's action, free of craving, is neither.

what a scholar hears: the commentary on 4.7 names four classes, black, black-white, white, and neither; the first three ripen, and the next sutra says only the impressions fit for their ripening come forward.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 4.7, Vyasa's commentary (the four classes of karma)
Bhagavad Gita 2.47 (your right is to the work, not its fruits)

notes: The four classes (black, black-white, white, neither) follow the Vyasa commentary as commonly summarized; confirm the description of 'white' as action through austerity, study and meditation, done inwardly.
'A gold chain still holds you' is the script's own image, not a quotation.
